sections.h2: Ways to sell a house in Lombard
sections.html:
Lombard sellers choose between a traditional listing, a for-sale-by-owner sale, and a cash purchase of the house as-is. The village, in DuPage County, runs permitting and code enforcement through its Community Development Department, and deeds are recorded by the DuPage County Recorder, so those two offices set most of the practical timeline.

The 2020 census counted 44,476 people in Lombard, and the mid-2025 estimate is 44,399.

Lombard began as Babcock's Grove, named for early settlers on the DuPage River, and took its present name from a Chicago developer who mapped the settlement in 1868. The Galena and Chicago Union Railroad arrived in 1848, and the village incorporated in 1869. The village calls itself the Lilac Village. A colonel's estate left to the village in 1927 became Lilacia Park, with some 200 varieties of lilac, and the Lilac Time festival and parade have run since 1930 into mid-May. A house near the park or the downtown station can use that identity in its listing description.

Rental housing is a big part of the market: 70.8 percent of homes are owner-occupied, the median home value is $335,700, and median gross rent is $1,948. There are 17,262 households averaging 2.48 people, and median household income is $100,362.

The commute is short at 25.6 minutes on average. The Metra Union Pacific West Line connects the village to Ogilvie Transportation Center and out to Elburn, and the I-88 and I-355 corridors and Illinois Routes 38, 53, 56 and 64 serve drivers. Pace buses use Yorktown Center as a hub, and the Illinois Prairie Path and Great Western Trail run through on former rail lines.

Mention the walk to the train, the trails and the park in your listing, because commuters and trail users are the buyers who value them most.

The village's fiscal year 2024 financial report cites a 9.79 percent increase in equalized assessed valuation, with new construction adding $5.06 million. Redevelopment projects near Yorktown Center include Lilac Station, Yorktown Reserve and the Summit at Yorktown.

Assessed value is one input to property tax bills, so ask the DuPage County Treasurer and Supervisor of Assessments for your parcel's current numbers before you set a price.

sections.h2: Which Lombard schools do buyers ask about?
sections.html:
Lombard's public high schools belong to Glenbard Township High School District 87, shared with Glen Ellyn, and Glenbard East High School is in the village. Elementary and middle schools (kindergarten through grade 8) belong to Lombard School District 44 or DuPage School District 45, depending on the street.

Line up the elementary district for your address before the first showing, since it shapes which families look at the house.

The Building Division handles signs, fire, fill and grade, new buildings, additions, backyard chickens, accessory structures and alterations. Permits can be requested online through the village portal, fees are paid when the permit is ready for pickup, and some items such as residential driveways, fences and new roofs carry flat rates. The division's number is (630) 620-5750.

  • Fences and grading: a permit is required for all fences and for all grading.
  • Exterior upkeep: grass and weeds must stay under eight inches during the growing season, and litter must be cleared within seven days.
  • Vehicles: inactive vehicles must be garaged and RVs may not sit in the front yard from November 1 through March 31.
  • Rentals: owners who rent must supply heat at 68 degrees from September 15 through June 1.
  • Address numbers: they must be visible and legible from the street.

A walk-through for these items before listing can head off an inspector's note. Lombard is a non-home-rule municipality with a council-manager government, so check the village code for local rules before you assume a state rule is the only one.

Owners should also keep waste containers covered, keep items on the parkway only within 24 hours of scheduled pickup, and park vehicles on an approved hard surface, not on grass. Commercial-size trucks are barred from residential districts. Tidy these before photographs, since a neighbor's complaint can bring an inspection.

Lombard's older core grew up around its railroad. Stops on the old Chicago Aurora and Elgin line once sat at Stewart Avenue, Main Street, Brewster Avenue and Westmore and Meyers Road. Cartoonist Harold Gray drew Little Orphan Annie in a restored Italianate house from 1881 on Main Street, and the Maple Street Chapel (1870) served as the first town hall and library. Landmarks like these give streets a recognizable identity that buyers notice.

sections.h2: Recording with the DuPage County Recorder
sections.html:
The DuPage County Recorder maintains the county's land records back to 1839, and recording is fee-funded. The fee for a deed (Document Class 1) is $86, which includes $10 for document storage, $21 for GIS, $1 for the real property fee and $18 for the Rental Housing Support Program. The Recorder's office number is 630-407-5400.

The state transfer tax in 35 ILCS 200/31-10 runs fifty cents per $500 block of declared value, and 35 ILCS 200/31-25 requires a declaration signed by at least one seller and one buyer. Collection of the tax runs through the recorder, and the statute phases out paper revenue stamps in favor of electronic stamps or other indicia. Ask your closing agent whether the village or county adds any local fee on your parcel.

Most delays in a Lombard sale come from a handful of items that can be settled in a week or two.

  1. Walk the house with the permit and code list above in hand, and fix or disclose anything an inspector might note.
  2. Find permit records for any fence, driveway, roof or alteration, since the Building Division at (630) 620-5750 can tell you what is on file.
  3. Ask the DuPage County Treasurer about your current tax balance.
  4. Agree on a written closing date and who pays each recording item.
  5. Sign the state declaration, with a signature from at least one seller and one buyer, and send it with the deed to the DuPage County Recorder.

sections.h2: When does a cash sale suit a Lombard owner?
sections.html:
A cash sale suits owners who need to sell a house with deferred repairs, a tenant situation or an inherited estate without staging and showings. With median rent near $1,948, landlords holding an older Lombard rental sometimes prefer a clean exit over renovating. Ask any buyer for a written closing date and a list of who pays each recording item before you sign.

A cash sale also skips the lender's appraisal and loan approval, so a deed that is ready to record is usually the only thing the timeline waits on.

faqs.q: Which office records my deed in Lombard?
faqs.a: The DuPage County Recorder, whose records start in 1839. The deed fee includes storage, GIS, real property and Rental Housing Support Program amounts. Call 630-407-5400 for questions.

faqs.q: Is a fence permit required in Lombard?
faqs.a: Yes. Permits are required for all fences so the homeowner knows the requirements before buying the fence. Fences are among the flat-rate permits.

faqs.q: Can I park an RV in my front yard in winter?
faqs.a: No. RVs are not permitted in the front yard from November 1 through March 31, and vehicles that are not street ready must be garaged.
Glenbard East High School in Lombard belongs to Glenbard Township High School District 87. Elementary students attend Lombard School District 44 or DuPage School District 45 depending on the street.

faqs.q: What is the Illinois transfer tax rate?
faqs.a: The statute at 35 ILCS 200/31-10 sets it, counted in $500 units of the value on the declaration. A mortgage that stays on the property is left out of the base.
